summary:
POLARIS Module is a browser-based planner for astronaut walks on Mars (EVAs), built on real NASA data for one site: a 1 × 1 km area of Pahrump Hills in Gale Crater, studied closely by the Curiosity rover.

Every Mars EVA has to answer four questions at once:

Where can we walk?
Where should we go?
How long will it take?
Is there enough oxygen?
The data to answer them exists, but it is scattered across orbital terrain models, rover archives, science papers and NASA life-support documents. POLARIS Module combines them on one map:

HiRISE terrain and slope: a shortest route and a slope-aware route that avoids ground steeper than the planner's limit
Science suggestions: activities sourced from Curiosity's findings, chosen by objective and the equipment carried
EVA time estimate: walking and stop time
Oxygen estimate: shows where along the route each astronaut's oxygen budget runs out, using NASA's Mars consumption rate
The plan can be viewed in 3D, saved, and exported as a report that lists its sources and assumptions. The project turns scattered mission data into a traceable plan that answers all four questions together. It is a prototype, not a safety tool.
details:
What it does and how it works

POLARIS Module is a route planner for astronaut walks on Mars (EVAs). It runs in a web browser with nothing to install. It covers a 1 × 1 km area of Pahrump Hills in Gale Crater, a site Curiosity studied closely with drilling and chemistry measurements.

A planner places waypoints, or adds a science target with one click, and the app answers four questions together:

  • Where can we walk? Two routes are computed on a 5 m terrain grid using A* pathfinding. Shortest finds the shortest path over terrain with data. Slope-aware never enters ground steeper than the planner's slope limit, and it prefers gentler slopes. If no route fits, the limits are not relaxed; the app explains what blocks the route.
  • Where should we go? The planner picks a science objective (rock textures, past water activity or mineral diversity) and ticks the equipment the crew carries. The Science tab then suggests 14 activities, including photography stops, two orbital imaging candidates and four proposed rock-chip samples. Each one is linked to published Curiosity evidence and can be added to the route. An activity cannot be added if its equipment is missing.
  • How long will it take? The app gives distance, elevation gain and loss, an elevation profile, and a duration estimate based on walking speed and time at each stop.
  • Is there enough oxygen? The planner sets the usable oxygen each astronaut carries (default 0.54 kg, the EVA suit's primary supply). Using NASA's Mars closed-loop rate of 0.076 kg per hour and a 30-minute reserve, the map marks where each route's oxygen budget runs out, in 2D and 3D.

A globe in the map corner shows where the site is on Mars. The plan can be viewed on a 3D terrain model, saved as a mission, and exported as a printable or JSON report. The report lists every source, assumption and limitation.

Data

All data comes from NASA and published science:

  • Terrain and imagery: a HiRISE terrain model and images (NASA PDS, University of Arizona).
  • Rover data: Curiosity's positions and traverse (NASA MMGIS), its drill sites, and 104 APXS chemistry measurements (Berger 2020).
  • Science findings: the tridymite discovery at Buckskin and published studies used for the activities (McBride 2015, Rampe 2015).
  • Oxygen values: NASA's life-support baseline values (BVAD Rev2, 2022) and EVA suit documents.

The terrain was prepared in Python: cropped to 1 km² and resampled to a 200 × 200 grid. Slope is computed at the original 1 m resolution, and each 5 m cell keeps its steepest value, so a steep patch is never averaged away. Every data file is versioned, fingerprinted, and checked by the app against the terrain it belongs to.

Benefits and intended impact

Today, someone planning an EVA has to combine terrain, rover data, papers and life-support figures by hand. POLARIS Module puts them on one map. A crew or mission planner can then see how the four constraints affect each other: a safer route takes longer, and more science stops need more oxygen.

It can also be used for teaching, letting students explore real Mars data and see how terrain, science and life support shape exploration.

Tools and technologies

  • App: TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet (2D map) and Three.js (3D terrain).
  • Data preparation: Python with NumPy and Pillow.
  • Quality: 265 automated tests (Vitest) and linting with ESLint.
  • Hosting: GitHub, with the live demo on GitHub Pages.
  • No special hardware is needed. The code is open source under the MIT License.

What makes it creative

  • It treats Mars as a place to walk, not just a map to look at.
  • It plans for four constraints together rather than one at a time.
  • The oxygen estimate shows directly where on the ground a plan stops being possible.
  • Science suggestions are tied to real rover findings and to the equipment carried, so every stop has a scientific reason and a source.

What the team considered

  • Honesty about limits. Slope limits, walking speed and oxygen values are scenario assumptions, not certified safety limits. The oxygen marker is where the planning reserve begins, not where oxygen runs out. The app and every report say this.
  • Traceability. Every layer, activity and oxygen value links to its source. We keep evidence separate from our own proposals.
  • Accuracy over averages. Slope keeps the worst case in each cell, cells without data are never crossed, and limits are never silently relaxed.
  • Accessibility. The app works on phones, can be used with the keyboard, and runs offline once built.
